content: #1 I am not (yet) a mathematician, so this might or might not be an at all insightful inquiry. I am curious on your thoughts of materialism/reductionism in structuralist disciplines such as higher category theory. I for one am not a fan of the model theoretical approach, that (for instance) a hom-set in some category can be a pure set of arbitrary symbols and all that matters is the algebraic axioms of composition, unity et cetera. For me it bothers me if a morphism of the hom-set is something such as {∅,{∅}} rather than an urelement/atom because even though it satisfies all the algebraic axioms and I can just pretend it be some morphism between objects, the internal structure of its alphabetical character is not conducive to the entity itself. I don't know, maybe this is is not at all precise and just a personal grievance.
subject: Thoughts on Reductionism in Mathematics

content:
#2 Reductionism in mathematics is just false sociologically. You can’t reduce all of mathematics down to a single theory and get the rest of the mathematics community to agree with your choice of theory, and the evidence comes from the century long debate over which foundations of mathematics should be taken to be the true foundations of mathematics that everything else must reduce down to. At some point, one has to conclude that they are all equally valid as foundations of mathematics each used by different subfields of mathematics, which then defeats the whole purpose of reductionism.

If it bothers you that ZFC only uses pure sets, you don’t have to use ZFC as your foundations of mathematics. You can use some membership based set theory with urelements. You can also use a function based set theory like ETCS + replacement where the theory makes a clean distinction between sets and functions and where elements are considered to be certain functions. You can also use higher order logic or dependent type theory. Most everything in mathematics will still work in those other foundations of mathematics.

As for model theory specifically, I think there has been structural approaches to model theory - for example categorical model theory, starting from Makkai and Paré’s 1989 paper titled “Accessible categories: the foundations of categorical model theory”. There is nothing intrinsic “pure set” about model theory, that’s just a result of most model theory texts being written using an membership based set theory as the underlying foundations and talking about membership based set theory as the foundations whose models one should study.
subject: Thoughts on Reductionism in Mathematics
